prompt: What does Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) protect in Azure SQL?
choices: Data at rest — the database files and its backups
Only the specific columns marked as sensitive
Only the data while it is in transit to the client
Only the query results shown to unprivileged users
correctAnswers: Data at rest — the database files and its backups
explanation: TDE encrypts the whole database at rest — files and backups — transparently to the application, and it is on by default. It protects against stolen files, whereas it does nothing against an authorised query: the engine decrypts pages as it reads them, so a DBA still sees plaintext.

prompt: What does Always Encrypted protect, and from whom?
choices: Specific columns end-to-end, hidden from the engine
The whole database at rest, transparently to the app
Only the values displayed in a query result set
The traffic between the client and the server
correctAnswers: Specific columns end-to-end, hidden from the engine
explanation: Always Encrypted protects specific columns end to end, with the key held by the client, so the engine and its administrators never see plaintext. TDE is the tempting alternative because it also encrypts, however TDE decrypts inside the engine and therefore cannot hide anything from a legitimate query.

prompt: What does dynamic data masking actually do?
choices: Obscures values in results; stored data is unchanged
Encrypts the sensitive columns where they sit at rest today
Permanently deletes the sensitive data from the table
Stops everyone, admins included, from ever seeing it
correctAnswers: Obscures values in results; stored data is unchanged
explanation: Masking obscures values in query results for non-privileged users, whereas the stored data is untouched. That is why it is not a security boundary: anyone with UNMASK, or a patient attacker running range queries, recovers the real value.

prompt: Which Azure SQL feature does NOT stop a privileged DBA from reading the real underlying values?
choices: Dynamic data masking on the column
Always Encrypted on the column
Neither offers any protection at all
Both stop a DBA equally well
correctAnswers: Dynamic data masking on the column
explanation: Dynamic data masking only alters results for non-privileged users, so a sufficiently privileged DBA still reads the real value. Always Encrypted is the one that stops them, because the key never reaches the engine — answering "both stop a DBA equally" is the belief that leaves sensitive columns exposed.

prompt: Which feature is recommended for columns like national ID or payment-card numbers where even admins must not see plaintext?
choices: Always Encrypted on the column
Dynamic data masking on the column
Transparent Data Encryption alone
Database auditing on its own
correctAnswers: Always Encrypted on the column
explanation: National ID and payment-card columns are exactly the case Always Encrypted exists for: the risk is insider and administrator access, not stolen files. Masking is the tempting cheaper option, but it is cosmetic and cannot withstand a privileged account.

prompt: What is the benefit of enabling Microsoft Entra database authentication for Azure SQL?
choices: Entra identities and groups instead of SQL logins
It encrypts every column in the database automatically
It removes the overhead that auditing would add
It is required before TDE can be turned on at all
correctAnswers: Entra identities and groups instead of SQL logins
explanation: Entra database authentication brings SQL access under the same identity governance as the rest of Azure — groups, Conditional Access, access reviews — instead of per-server SQL logins. It is unrelated to encryption, which is the usual conflation: it changes who gets in rather than how data is stored.

prompt: Which setting disables SQL logins entirely, allowing only Microsoft Entra authentication?
choices: Support only Microsoft Entra authentication
Set the Microsoft Entra admin for the server first
Enable Transparent Data Encryption on it
Enable Always Encrypted on the columns
correctAnswers: Support only Microsoft Entra authentication
explanation: Support only Microsoft Entra authentication disables SQL logins entirely. Setting the Entra admin is the closest miss and only a prerequisite: it enables Entra sign-in alongside SQL logins, whereas this setting is what removes the SQL path.

prompt: Where can Azure SQL database auditing send recorded events?
choices: A workspace, a storage account, or Event Hubs
Auditing has no configurable destination at all
Only a local file on the SQL server itself
Only to Microsoft Support, upon request
correctAnswers: A workspace, a storage account, or Event Hubs
explanation: Auditing can target a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account or Event Hubs, and the choice drives cost and queryability. It is never a local file on the server, which is the on-premises habit worth unlearning — there is no server filesystem to write to.

prompt: Is Transparent Data Encryption enabled by default on new Azure SQL databases?
choices: Yes, on by default
Only with Always Encrypted
Only on Managed Instance
No, enable it by hand
correctAnswers: Yes, on by default
explanation: TDE is on by default for new Azure SQL databases and Managed Instances, using a Microsoft-managed key. Believing it must be enabled manually is the misconception that leads teams to deploy something they already have, whereas a customer-managed key is the optional upgrade.

prompt: Where does the decryption key live when using Always Encrypted?
choices: Entirely on the client, never given to the engine
On the SQL server, stored alongside the data itself
In the database transaction log, for recovery
In the TDE protector held in Azure Key Vault
correctAnswers: Entirely on the client, never given to the engine
explanation: The Always Encrypted key lives entirely on the client and is never given to the engine, which is precisely what hides plaintext from administrators. The TDE protector in Key Vault is the tempting answer because it is also a key in a vault, however that one is used by the engine itself.

prompt: Where do you set the Microsoft Entra admin for an Azure SQL logical server?
choices: SQL server ▸ Microsoft Entra ID ▸ Set admin
Key Vault ▸ Access configuration ▸ Access policies
Defender for Cloud ▸ Environment settings
The database ▸ Dynamic Data Masking blade
correctAnswers: SQL server ▸ Microsoft Entra ID ▸ Set admin
explanation: The Entra admin is set at the logical server level, under Microsoft Entra ID. It is not a database-level setting, which is the common misclick: the databases inherit it, whereas the assignment itself cannot be made on one of them.

prompt: Of TDE, Always Encrypted, and dynamic data masking, which is NOT a form of encryption?
choices: Dynamic data masking of results
Transparent Data Encryption at rest
Always Encrypted on the columns
All three are equally strong
correctAnswers: Dynamic data masking of results
explanation: Masking is the one that is not encryption: it changes what is displayed, whereas the stored bytes are unaltered. Treating all three as equally strong is the answer that matters most to reject, because it is what leads to masking being used where Always Encrypted was required.

prompt: A support team needs to query a customer table for troubleshooting, but card numbers must not appear in their results, with no application changes. Which feature fits best?
choices: Dynamic data masking
Always Encrypted on the columns
Transparent Data Encryption
Database auditing alone
correctAnswers: Dynamic data masking
explanation: Masking lets a support team query the table while sensitive values come back obscured, with no change to the application or the stored data. Always Encrypted is the tempting stronger option, but it would break the troubleshooting use case — the support team could not read anything at all.

prompt: TDE protects backups and files at rest but would NOT prevent which of the following?
choices: A DBA with query access reading the values in plaintext
An attacker who steals a backup file from the storage account
An attacker who steals the raw database files
Data exposure if a disk is physically removed
correctAnswers: A DBA with query access reading the values in plaintext
explanation: TDE is transparent to authorised queries, so a DBA with query access still sees plaintext column values. The three distractors are all at-rest scenarios — stolen files, stolen backups, a removed disk — which is exactly what TDE does cover, whereas the insider case needs Always Encrypted.

prompt: Which control gives the compliance team a record of WHO queried a sensitive table and WHEN?
choices: Database auditing
Always Encrypted keys
Dynamic data masking
Encryption at rest
correctAnswers: Database auditing
explanation: Auditing is what records who did what and when, which is the only one of these that produces evidence. The encryption options are tempting because they sound stronger, however none of them logs anything: they change what an attacker can read rather than what you can prove afterwards.

prompt: Which is a valid caution before enabling 'Support only Microsoft Entra authentication'?
choices: It disables SQL logins, so apps using them break
It disables Transparent Data Encryption on the server
It permanently deletes the SQL logins, unrecoverably
It requires Always Encrypted to be configured first
correctAnswers: It disables SQL logins, so apps using them break
explanation: Enabling Entra-only authentication disables SQL logins outright, so any application still using one stops working. It does not delete the logins irrecoverably, which is the exaggerated fear — but the outage is real, so verify dependencies before flipping it.

prompt: Which feature would you use to centralize SQL access on corporate group membership rather than individual database logins?
choices: Microsoft Entra authentication with a group
Transparent Data Encryption on the whole database
A shared SQL login used by the whole team
Dynamic data masking on the columns
correctAnswers: Microsoft Entra authentication with a group
explanation: Entra authentication with an Entra group as the admin centralises SQL access on corporate group membership, so joining and leaving the group is the whole lifecycle. A shared SQL login is the tempting operational shortcut and it is the practice being replaced: it cannot be tied to a person or revoked individually.

prompt: A requirement states sensitive data must be encrypted such that a cloud operator with full server access still cannot read it. Which feature is required?
choices: Always Encrypted on the column
Database auditing to a workspace
Dynamic data masking of results
Transparent Data Encryption
correctAnswers: Always Encrypted on the column
explanation: A requirement naming a cloud operator with server access describes Always Encrypted, because the key stays client-side and the operator never has it. TDE is the tempting answer since it is the encryption that is already on, however the engine decrypts for it — so anyone querying through the engine reads plaintext.

prompt: Which statement about TDE and Always Encrypted used together is correct?
choices: Complementary: TDE at rest, Always Encrypted per column
They are mutually exclusive and cannot both be turned on
Always Encrypted replaces the need for TDE entirely
TDE encrypts columns end-to-end, so AE is redundant
correctAnswers: Complementary: TDE at rest, Always Encrypted per column
explanation: They are complementary and routinely used together: TDE covers everything at rest, Always Encrypted covers named columns end to end. Believing one replaces the other is the trap, since they defend against different attackers — stolen media versus a privileged insider.

prompt: Server-level auditing is already enabled on an Azure SQL server. A database-level audit policy is then enabled on one of its databases. What happens to that database’s audit events?
choices: Both levels log it, so the event appears twice
The database-level policy silently supersedes the server one
The server policy stops applying to that database
Auditing is rejected until one policy is removed
correctAnswers: Both levels log it, so the event appears twice
explanation: Server-level auditing applies to every database on the server, so a database-level policy added on top makes each event logged twice rather than once. The tempting answer is that the database policy supersedes the server one — it does not; the two are independent, which is why auditing at the server level alone is the recommendation.

prompt: What is TDE transparent TO?
choices: The application — no change to read or write
Administrators — they cannot see any of the data
The storage layer — it bypasses disk encryption
The network — it encrypts the data in transit
correctAnswers: The application — no change to read or write
explanation: TDE encrypts/decrypts at the I/O level, transparent to the application; it does not address in-transit or admin-visibility concerns.

prompt: A security review flags that dynamic data masking was chosen to 'protect' SSNs from database administrators. Why is this inappropriate?
choices: Masking only hides values for non-privileged users
Masking permanently encrypts the SSNs, breaking the app
Masking cannot be applied to a text column at all
Masking requires Always Encrypted in order to work
correctAnswers: Masking only hides values for non-privileged users
explanation: Masking is a convenience control, not a cryptographic boundary; Always Encrypted is the correct tool against admin access.

prompt: Which Azure SQL protection is enabled by default and requires no application awareness?
choices: Transparent Data Encryption
Always Encrypted on the column
Microsoft Entra-only auth
Dynamic data masking
correctAnswers: Transparent Data Encryption
explanation: TDE is on by default and transparent to applications, so it needs no code change. Always Encrypted is the tempting answer because it is the stronger control, however it requires client driver and key configuration — and masking and Entra-only auth both need deliberate setup too.

prompt: To investigate a suspected data-exfiltration incident, which SQL feature provides the evidence trail?
choices: Database auditing to a Log Analytics workspace
Transparent Data Encryption on the whole database
Dynamic data masking on the queried columns
Always Encrypted with keys held on the client
correctAnswers: Database auditing to a Log Analytics workspace
explanation: Auditing records the queries and access events needed for an investigation; the encryption/masking features do not produce an activity trail.

prompt: Which two statements about encryption at rest and masking in Azure SQL Database are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: Transparent Data Encryption encrypts the whole database at rest
Always Encrypted hides column data from database administrators
Dynamic data masking is a strong cryptographic boundary against admins
Transparent Data Encryption is disabled by default
correctAnswers: Transparent Data Encryption encrypts the whole database at rest
Always Encrypted hides column data from database administrators
explanation: TDE encrypts the whole database at rest and Always Encrypted hides column data from administrators. Neither distractor holds: TDE is enabled by default rather than disabled, and masking is a display filter rather than a cryptographic boundary.

prompt: Which two statements about Always Encrypted key handling, audit sinks, and Entra-only authentication are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: Always Encrypted keeps its key on the client side
Database auditing can target Event Hubs as a sink
Entra-only authentication is easily reversible, safely
Dynamic data masking permanently modifies data
correctAnswers: Always Encrypted keeps its key on the client side
Database auditing can target Event Hubs as a sink
explanation: Always Encrypted keeps its key client-side, and auditing can target Event Hubs. The two false options are the ones worth naming: Entra-only authentication does break applications still using SQL logins, whereas masking never modifies stored data.

prompt: Which two threats does Always Encrypted specifically address that TDE does not? (Choose two.)
choices: A database administrator reading the column values
A cloud operator with server access reading plaintext
Theft of a raw backup file sitting at rest in a container
Physical theft of the underlying disk itself
correctAnswers: A database administrator reading the column values
A cloud operator with server access reading plaintext
explanation: Always Encrypted adds protection against a DBA and against a cloud operator reading plaintext — both insiders who query through the engine. Stolen backups and stolen disks are the tempting picks, however TDE already covers those, which is the whole reason the two features coexist.

prompt: Referring to requirement 5 (national ID columns must remain unreadable in plaintext even to database administrators), which feature should Northwind use?
choices: Always Encrypted on the column
Dynamic data masking on the column
Transparent Data Encryption alone
Database auditing on its own
correctAnswers: Always Encrypted on the column
explanation: Only Always Encrypted keeps plaintext away from the engine and from administrators, which is what "unreadable in the database" requires. TDE alone is the tempting answer because it is already on, but it decrypts transparently for any authorised query.

prompt: Referring to requirement 6 (compliance must review a full history of who queried a sensitive table and when), which feature should Northwind enable?
choices: Database auditing
Always Encrypted keys
Dynamic data masking
Encryption at rest
correctAnswers: Database auditing
explanation: A history of who queried what is auditing, and nothing else here produces a record. The encryption options are tempting because they feel like stronger controls, whereas neither of them logs access — they change readability rather than accountability.

prompt: Northwind also wants to stop using individual SQL logins and instead govern database access through corporate identities and groups. What should they implement?
choices: Microsoft Entra authentication, with groups as users
Transparent Data Encryption with a customer-managed key
A shared SQL login for the whole team to use
Dynamic data masking on the login table
correctAnswers: Microsoft Entra authentication, with groups as users
explanation: Entra authentication with an admin and groups moves SQL access onto corporate identities, and Entra-only enforcement can then retire the SQL logins entirely. A shared SQL login is the practice being replaced, since it cannot be attributed to a person or revoked for one.

prompt: Order the steps to enforce Microsoft Entra-only authentication on an Azure SQL server.
reorderItems: Set a Microsoft Entra admin for the SQL server
Confirm all applications have migrated off SQL logins
Verify SQL logins can no longer authenticate
explanation: An Entra admin must exist and applications must be migrated before SQL logins are disabled, or the switch locks out both administrators and apps. Disabling first is the ordering mistake, and it is not easily reversible under time pressure — which is why the migration step comes before it rather than after.

prompt: Order the steps to protect a national-ID column so even DBAs cannot see it in plaintext.
reorderItems: Configure Always Encrypted for that column with a client-side key
Store the column encryption key in Key Vault
Update client applications to use an Always Encrypted-enabled driver
explanation: The column encryption key and the encrypted column must be defined before applications can be pointed at the encryption-aware driver. Updating the applications first is the tempting parallel-track approach, however there is nothing for the driver to decrypt yet, so the change cannot be validated.

prompt: Configure this simplified Azure SQL security screen for a table with card numbers, where a support team must query it without seeing card numbers, and compliance needs an audit trail.
explanation: Masking hides card numbers from the support team's results, TDE stays on for at-rest protection, and auditing records who queried what — three controls answering three different questions. Reaching for Always Encrypted here is the trap, because it would stop the support team reading anything at all.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable database auditing sending events to a Log Analytics workspace. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: Auditing to a Log Analytics workspace records logins and queries in a queryable destination, which is exactly the compliance trail requested. Note the cost consequence it carries: the workspace bills for ingestion and retention, so the destination choice is not neutral.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable dynamic data masking on all sensitive columns. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: Masking hides values in results, whereas it records nothing about who queried what or when — so it produces no audit trail at all. It is the tempting answer because it visibly does something to sensitive data, which is not the same as accounting for access to it.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable Transparent Data Encryption. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: TDE protects data at rest and logs nothing, so it cannot provide an audit trail. It is tempting because it is the encryption that is already enabled and feels like baseline compliance, however compliance here asked for evidence of access rather than protection of storage.

prompt: Complete the command that makes the Entra group SecAdmins the Microsoft Entra administrator of SQL server sql1.
template: az sql server [[b1]] create --server sql1 --resource-group RG1 --display-name SecAdmins --object-id [[b2]]
explanation: A server has exactly one Entra administrator, which is why pointing it at a GROUP is how several people hold the role — and the group is identified by its object ID, not by the display name, which is merely a label on the assignment. `ad-only-auth` is the closest miss and is the separate switch that disables SQL logins; running it before an Entra admin exists is what locks everyone out of the server.

prompt: Build the sequence that moves SQL server sql1 to Entra-only authentication without losing access to it. Not every action in the pool belongs in the answer.
poolItems: Set an Entra group as the server’s Microsoft Entra administrator, so that several named people hold the role
Create contained Entra database users for the applications that still connect
Enable Entra-only authentication on the server, which disables all SQL logins
Delete the server’s SQL administrator login
Disable the server's public network access
Enable auditing to a Log Analytics workspace
correctOrder: Set an Entra group as the server’s Microsoft Entra administrator, so that several named people hold the role
Create contained Entra database users for the applications that still connect
Enable Entra-only authentication on the server, which disables all SQL logins
explanation: Entra-only authentication disables every SQL login at once, including the server administrator, so the Entra admin must exist first and the applications must already have Entra database users — otherwise the switch is a self-inflicted outage that cannot be undone from inside the server. The distractors are things that feel like part of the same clean-up: deleting or rotating the SQL admin login is unnecessary because Entra-only already disables it, and network access and auditing are separate controls that do not affect authentication.

prompt: Complete the command that turns on auditing for database db1 and sends the audit events to a Log Analytics workspace.
template: az sql db audit-policy update --server sql1 --name db1 --resource-group RG1 --state Enabled [[b1]] [[b2]]
explanation: Auditing has three independent destinations — storage, Log Analytics and Event Hub — each with its own target-state switch, so `--state Enabled` alone turns auditing on with nowhere to write. The blob-storage variant is the tempting pick because storage is the older default, whereas it sends the events somewhere Sentinel and workbooks cannot query. The workspace is named by full resource ID rather than by name, since it may live in another resource group or subscription.

prompt: Which PowerShell cmdlet checks whether TDE is enabled on a database?
choices: Get-AzSqlDatabaseTransparentDataEncryption
Get-AzSqlServerTransparentDataEncryptionProtector
Get-AzSqlDatabaseTransparentDataEncryptionState
Get-AzSqlDatabaseEncryptionStatus
correctAnswers: Get-AzSqlDatabaseTransparentDataEncryption
explanation: Get-AzSqlDatabaseTransparentDataEncryption returns the TDE state. Get-AzSqlServerKeyVaultKey relates to BYOK keys for TDE, not its status; the other two don't exist.

prompt: Which PowerShell cmdlet sets the Microsoft Entra admin on a SQL server?
choices: Set-AzSqlServerActiveDirectoryAdministrator
Set-AzSqlInstanceActiveDirectoryAdministrator
Set-AzSqlServerAzureADAdministrator
Set-AzSqlServerEntraAdministrator
correctAnswers: Set-AzSqlServerActiveDirectoryAdministrator
explanation: Set-AzSqlServerActiveDirectoryAdministrator is the real cmdlet (the module still uses the ActiveDirectory naming). The other three don't exist.
